title: The Black Count: Glory, Revolution, Betrayal, and the Real Count of Monte Cristo
author: Tom Reiss
target_audience: Readers interested in history and biography
Fans of Alexandre Dumas and classic literature
Scholars and students of the French Revolution
Those exploring narratives of race and social mobility
primary_purpose: To reveal the life story of General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, a man of color who rose to the highest ranks of the French military during the Revolution, and who inspired his son Alexandre Dumas to write literary classics, while examining issues of race, power, and legacy in French and world history.

structure_format.narrative_style: Detailed, engaging, and novelistic historical nonfiction
structure_format.organization: Chronological narrative structured around General Dumas’s life, supplemented by historical context, archival research, and contemporary perspectives
features: Comparisons to literary works by Alexandre Dumas
In-depth analysis of race and identity in revolutionary France

key_concepts_lessons: General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas broke barriers as the son of an enslaved woman and a white nobleman, rising to become a celebrated general in revolutionary France.
His life illustrates both the possibilities of social upheaval and the persistent dangers of racism and betrayal—even in revolutionary societies claiming equality.
Personal integrity and heroism can clash with political expediency and prejudice.
Racial identity played a critical role in both Dumas’s rise and downfall amid changing political tides.
Thomas-Alexandre Dumas’s extraordinary story directly influenced his son’s literary masterpieces, including 'The Count of Monte Cristo'.
notable_features: Winner of the Pulitzer Prize for Biography
First comprehensive biography of General Dumas in English
Blend of military history, social analysis, and literary connections
Focus on both individual life and broader historical movements
cultural_historical_context: Set against the backdrop of late 18th-century France: the waning ancien régime, violent upheaval of the Revolution, rise of Napoleon, and changes in attitudes toward race, slavery, and equality. Published in 2012 amid renewed scholarly and popular interest in underrepresented historical figures of color.
reception_impact: Won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography in 2013
Acclaimed for bringing a forgotten figure to public attention and illuminating issues of race and identity in European history
Praised for its engaging narrative and meticulous research
Inspired discussions on the intersection of literature, history, and race

The Slave Who Defeated Napoleon: Toussaint Louverture and the Haitian War of Independence by Philippe Girard
